meaning: The Divine Name; not a label but the living presence/reality of the Divine, realized through remembrance.

etymology.note: A pan-Indian root shared by nearly every devotional (Bhakti) tradition, not coined by Sikhi. Gurbani takes the ordinary word for 'name' and elevates it into a theological category: the Name as accessible form of the otherwise formless Divine.

context.note: Used identically across Guru Bani and Bhagat Bani because 'Naam-simran' (remembrance of the Name) was the shared vocabulary of the whole Sant/Bhakti movement before and during Guru Nanak's time. Kabir ji's usage draws on his own Sant-Bhasha Bhakti idiom, not on Punjabi court language — so the word's charge comes from that Bhakti stream, which Gurbani absorbs directly.

usageInContext.note: The word does not carry one fixed weight — in verses about separation (viyog) it marks the ache of felt absence; in verses about union (milaap) it names felt presence itself. Reading 'Naam' correctly means noticing which emotional register the surrounding lines are in, not applying one dictionary gloss everywhere.
usageInContext.source: recurring pattern across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: a felt state of connectedness (or its ache in absence), not a fixed label — the same word marks opposite emotional poles depending on the shabad it sits in

usageInContext.note: The rahao (refrain) line of Sukhmani Sahib names Naam as 'amrit' and as what gives the devotee's mind rest — tying this entry directly to Amrit rather than leaving 'Naam' as an abstract label.
usageInContext.source: Sukhmani Sahib, opening Rahao
usageInContext.pankti: ਸੁਖਮਨੀ ਸੁਖ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਨਾਮੁ ॥ ਭਗਤ ਜਨਾ ਕੈ ਮਨਿ ਬਿਸ੍ਰਾਮੁ ॥ ਰਹਾਉ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: God's Name is the nectar of peace
usageInContext.bhavarth: Naam identified directly with Amrit (nectar) and with the devotee's inner rest — the whole of Sukhmani Sahib is framed as an unpacking of this one line

interpretations.view: Reads 'Naam' as lived awareness of Hukam — the Divine Order operating through creation and one's own life — rather than a word or sound to be repeated. On this reading, Naam-simran is training attention to stay aware of that Order, not a ritual chant.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact wording against his own lectures on Naam before quoting it as his.

meaning: The Divine Order/Will — the underlying law by which all of creation moves; also, ordinary 'command' in Persian-derived usage.

etymology.note: Entered Punjabi through the Persian-administered courts and chancery language of medieval Punjab, where 'hukam' meant a ruler's decree. Guru Nanak takes this everyday administrative/Mughal-era word and reuses it for cosmic order — 'hukam rajai chalna' (walking in step with the Order) in Japji Sahib — rather than substituting a native Sanskrit-Punjabi term.

context.note: A clear case where the historical/political language of the era (Persian court idiom) supplies the word, and Gurbani keeps that Persian shape rather than Sanskritizing it.

usageInContext.note: 'Hukam' is defined relationally, in the very same couplet, against 'Haumai': recognizing that all things stand within the Order is what directly loosens the sense of separate self. The two words are explained by their effect on each other, not in isolation.
usageInContext.source: Japji Sahib, Pauri 1
usageInContext.pankti: ਹੁਕਮੈ ਅੰਦਰਿ ਸਭੁ ਕੋ ਬਾਹਰਿ ਹੁਕਮਿ ਨ ਕੋਇ ॥ ਨਾਨਕ ਹੁਕਮੈ ਜੇ ਬੁਝੈ ਤ ਹਉਮੈ ਕਹੈ ਨ ਕੋਇ ॥੧॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: all things stand within the Order; none stand outside it
usageInContext.bhavarth: grasping Hukam is not separate from losing Haumai — one word's realization is the other word's dissolution

interpretations.view: Reads 'Hukam' as the observable law/order running through nature and one's own circumstances, to be understood by reasoning about cause and effect — not as a mysterious fatalistic decree accepted on faith alone.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact wording against his lectures on Japji Sahib before quoting it as his.

meaning: The Word — both a hymn/composition in Gurbani and, philosophically, the divine sound/vibration through which truth is revealed.

etymology.note: Carries the older Indian philosophical charge of śabda-brahman (reality as sound/word), a concept already current in Vedantic and Bhakti thought before Guru Nanak. Kabir ji's shabads use the same weight of the term — the Word as guide — showing the concept is inherited, then re-centered on the Guru's Word.

context.note: Consistent across all contributors to Guru Granth Sahib; each author's 'shabad' still means their own hymn, but the underlying concept of Shabad-as-truth is common Sant-tradition ground, not Punjabi-specific.

usageInContext.note: The same word denotes both a single composition ("a shabad of the Guru") and the philosophical Word-principle. Which sense is meant is only clear from context: a sentence about singing or recitation points to the first sense, a sentence about the nature of truth points to the second.
usageInContext.source: general usage pattern across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: a specific hymn, or the underlying principle of the Word
usageInContext.bhavarth: context — is the line talking about music/recitation, or about ultimate reality? — decides which of the two senses applies

interpretations.view: Emphasizes reading a shabad primarily through its own internal logic and through parallel shabads elsewhere in Guru Granth Sahib ("Gurbani viakhya Gurbani ton" — let Gurbani interpret Gurbani), rather than through later external commentary layered on top of it.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known methodological position, not a specific quote — verify against his own talks.

meaning: The Formless One — God without shape or physical form.

etymology.note: A transparent Sanskrit compound. The 'formless God' idea is central to Nirguna Bhakti generally (Kabir uses 'Nirakar' too), so the word and the concept both predate their specific use in Gurbani.

context.note: Featured in the Mool Mantar tradition of describing God's attributes; the term is shared vocabulary of the Nirguna (formless-God) wing of the Bhakti movement rather than a Sikhi coinage.

usageInContext.note: Sits inside a connected chain of attributes in the Mool Mantar — Nirbhau (fearless), Nirvair (without enmity), Akal Murat (beyond time), Ajooni (unborn), Saibhang (self-existent). Its meaning is best read as one link in that chain rather than a standalone definition.
usageInContext.source: Mool Mantar
usageInContext.pankti: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: without form (implied by "Akal Murat, Ajooni" — beyond time, unborn)
usageInContext.bhavarth: one attribute in a linked list defining what God is not, each word sharpening the one before it

interpretations.view: Treats 'Nirankar' as a doctrinal statement ruling out any physical form or idol for God, used argumentatively against image-worship rather than as a merely poetic description.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact framing against his lectures before quoting it as his.

meaning: Wondrous Lord/Teacher — the most common Sikh name for God, an exclamation of wonder joined to the word for Guru.

breakdown.meaning: "wondrous, wow" — a Persian exclamation of awe/praise

etymology.note: A genuine hybrid: a Persian exclamation of astonishment fused to a Sanskrit title of reverence. Its crystallization as the Sikh name for God is documented in Bhai Gurdas Ji's writings, reflecting Punjab's everyday bilingual Persian–Sanskrit speech of the period rather than either language alone.

context.note: Not found as a fixed compound in the Guru Granth Sahib itself in this exact liturgical sense; it develops as living Sikh usage alongside the scripture, so its 'old-times' context is the spoken Persian-Punjabi of the Guru era, not classical Sanskrit scripture.

usageInContext.note: Because the compound is not found as such in Guru Granth Sahib, its relational meaning has to be traced through where it does live: Sikh ardas (supplication), kirtan refrains, and the greeting 'Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa' — contexts of address and exclamation, not scriptural exegesis of a single tuk.
usageInContext.source: Sikh liturgical and devotional usage (post-Gurbani)
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: an address of wonder to the Guru/God
usageInContext.bhavarth: functions as living, spoken devotion rather than as a term whose sense is fixed by one scriptural verse

interpretations.view: Treats 'Waheguru' as a contemplative address used in sustained remembrance, not a mantra expected to produce specific results by repetition alone.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact wording against his lectures before quoting it as his.

meaning: The True Guru/Teacher — used for God, the Guru's presence, or the ten Gurus.

etymology.note: A standard Sanskrit compound already used across Bhakti poetry — Kabir ji's dohas use 'Satguru' with the same sense of an inwardly truthful teacher, well before it became a core Sikh term.

context.note: Shows continuity between Kabir's Sant vocabulary and Gurbani's — the word doesn't need to be reinterpreted through Punjabi, it carries straight over from Sanskrit-rooted Bhakti idiom.

usageInContext.note: Very often paired with 'seva' — "Satgur ki seva" (service/devotion to the True Guru) — so the word's practical, relational meaning is inseparable from what one does in response to it, not just what it names.
usageInContext.source: recurring phrase pattern across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: a relationship enacted through seva, not only a title held by a person

usageInContext.note: Opens Anand Sahib by tying 'Satguru' directly to a felt result — bliss (anand) — rather than presenting the term abstractly. The line reports an event ('I have found the Satguru') before saying anything descriptive about what a Satguru is.
usageInContext.source: Anand Sahib, opening line
usageInContext.pankti: ਅਨੰਦੁ ਭਇਆ ਮੇਰੀ ਮਾਏ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਮੈ ਪਾਇਆ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: Bliss has come, my mother — I have found the True Guru
usageInContext.bhavarth: Satguru defined by its effect (bliss/anand) rather than by a description of the Guru's qualities

interpretations.view: Emphasizes 'Satguru' as pointing primarily to true guidance/the Shabad-Guru itself, rather than to reverence for a person's personality — consistent with a broader rationalist caution against personality-centered devotion.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact wording against his lectures before quoting it as his.

meaning: One who is oriented toward, and lives by, the Guru's teaching — 'Guru-facing.'

etymology.note: A directional compound: literally 'facing the Guru.' The 'mukh' (face/orientation) construction mirrors a broader Indic pattern of describing spiritual disposition as which way one 'faces.'

context.note: Coined/used within Gurbani specifically as the theological counterpart to Manmukh; a Sikhi-specific pairing rather than inherited wholesale from earlier Bhakti authors.

usageInContext.note: Almost never defined alone in Gurbani — its meaning is drawn out by contrast with Manmukh in the same or neighboring lines. 'Facing the Guru' only means something concrete against its opposite, 'facing one's own mind.'
usageInContext.source: recurring Gurmukh/Manmukh contrast across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: one whose face is turned toward the Guru
usageInContext.bhavarth: an orientation of will, defined relationally against its opposite rather than as a standalone trait

meaning: One oriented toward their own mind/ego rather than the Guru — self-willed.

etymology.note: Built as the deliberate opposite of Gurmukh, using the same 'mukh' (facing) construction turned toward the self instead of the Guru.

context.note: Part of a Sikhi-specific conceptual pair; understanding it requires reading it against Gurmukh rather than in isolation.

usageInContext.note: Functions as the mirror-term to Gurmukh; wherever it appears, the surrounding lines are implicitly measuring the described person against Guru-oriented living, even when 'Gurmukh' itself isn't in the same line.
usageInContext.source: recurring Gurmukh/Manmukh contrast across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: one whose face is turned toward their own mind
usageInContext.bhavarth: a relational, not standalone, category — always implicitly measured against Gurmukh

meaning: Remembrance — the practice of keeping the Divine Name present in the mind.

etymology.note: Same root that gives 'smriti' (memory/remembered scripture) in wider Indian religious vocabulary. Its devotional sense — remembering God rather than merely recalling a fact — is a Bhakti-era development shared by Kabir, Ravidas, and Nanak alike.

context.note: A pan-Bhakti practice-word; Kabir ji's 'simran' and Guru Nanak's 'Naam simran' describe the same discipline inherited from the broader medieval devotional movement.

usageInContext.note: Almost always appears paired with 'Naam' rather than standing alone — the two words describe a single practice (remembering the Name) from two angles: 'Naam' names what is remembered, 'Simran' names the act of remembering.
usageInContext.source: recurring "Naam simran" phrase pattern
usageInContext.bhavarth: the active, ongoing discipline side of the Naam/Simran pair, rather than a one-time event

interpretations.view: Frames Simran as sustained inner awareness rather than a count of repetitions — the value is in the quality of attention, not the number of times a word is said.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact wording against his lectures before quoting it as his.

meaning: Devotion — loving, participatory devotion to the Divine.

etymology.rootForm: भक्ति (bhakti), from root भज् (bhaj) — "to share, partake, adore"
etymology.note: Predates Sikhi by centuries as the name of the whole pan-Indian Bhakti movement. When Kabir ji, Ravidas ji, or Namdev ji use 'bhagti,' they are using the movement's own founding term, which Guru Granth Sahib then incorporates directly through the inclusion of Bhagat Bani.

context.note: One of the clearest examples of a word whose meaning should be read through its Bhakti-movement origin rather than translated as a purely Punjabi/Sikh term.

usageInContext.note: Carries a caste-critical edge specifically in the Bhagat Bani of Ravidas ji and Namdev ji — both from communities excluded from temple worship — so 'bhagti' in their lines often implicitly asserts direct access to the Divine without priestly or caste intermediaries, a nuance lost if the word is read only as generic 'devotion.'
usageInContext.source: Bhagat Bani (Ravidas Ji, Namdev Ji) within Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: direct, unmediated access to the Divine — pointed, in these authors' mouths, against caste-based religious exclusion

meaning: Congregation — the company of the faithful gathered together; also 'Sadh Sangat,' company of the holy.

etymology.note: Reflects the broader Bhakti-era emphasis on 'satsang' (company of truth/truthful people); Gurbani's 'Sadh Sangat' is a direct continuation of that older devotional institution.

context.note: Institutionalized in Sikh practice (congregational worship), but the underlying word and the value placed on 'holy company' are shared with the wider Bhakti movement.

usageInContext.note: Regularly appears alongside Seva and Langar as one of a working trio — Sangat is who gathers, Seva is what is done, Langar is the meal shared — so isolating the word from that trio loses its institutional, practical meaning.
usageInContext.source: recurring pattern in Guru Nanak Dev Ji's and Guru Amar Das Ji's institution-building
usageInContext.bhavarth: one part of a practical trio (Sangat–Seva–Langar), not a purely devotional abstraction

usageInContext.note: Sukhmani Sahib's ashtpadi on the company of the holy states the effect directly and immediately — being in Sadh Sangat itself produces inner bliss — rather than describing Sangat's properties abstractly.
usageInContext.source: Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 7 (on the glory of Sadh Sangat)
usageInContext.pankti: ਸਾਧ ਕੈ ਸੰਗਿ ਮਨਿ ਹੋਇ ਅਨੰਦੁ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: In the Company of the Holy, the mind becomes blissful
usageInContext.bhavarth: Sangat's value is stated as a direct, felt effect on the mind, not a duty or abstract virtue

meaning: 'One, whose expression is Onkar' — the foundational statement of the oneness of God that opens Guru Granth Sahib.

breakdown.meaning: the sound/syllable Om given form as 'kar' (creator/creation), from Sanskrit Om + kāra

etymology.rootForm: एक (eka) + ओंकार (oṃkāra, from ओम् Om + कार kāra)
etymology.note: Onkar reworks the Vedic/Upanishadic primal syllable Om (the pranava, considered the sound-seed of creation) — Guru Nanak takes this ancient sacred sound and prefixes 'Ik' to assert numerical, exclusive oneness, sharpening a Vedantic symbol into an explicit monotheistic statement.

context.note: The clearest example of a word reaching back to Vedic/Upanishadic sound-symbolism (Om) rather than to Punjabi or Persian roots — its 'old times' context is classical Sanskrit cosmology.

usageInContext.note: Opens the entire Guru Granth Sahib and is followed immediately by a chain of further attributes (Sat Naam, Karta Purakh, Nirbhau, Nirvair, Akal Murat, Ajooni, Saibhang, Gur Prasad) — every later Mool Mantar term should be read as unpacking this opening numeral-symbol, not as separate from it.
usageInContext.source: Mool Mantar
usageInContext.pankti: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ ॥
usageInContext.bhavarth: the root statement that every following attribute in the Mool Mantar explains or defends

interpretations.view: Reads the numeral 'Ik' as a deliberate, argued assertion of strict oneness — a doctrinal claim against polytheistic and dualistic readings current at the time, not a decorative flourish.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position, broadly shared across reformist Sikh commentary — confirm his specific wording before quoting it as his.

meaning: Two distinct senses depending on origin: (1) 'action, deed, the moral law of cause and effect' (from Sanskrit); (2) 'grace, mercy, kindness' (from Persian/Arabic) — Gurbani most often uses the second sense for God's grace.

etymology.note: A word that looks single in Gurmukhi script but is actually two separate loanwords that happened to converge in sound. Reading Gurbani correctly requires knowing which root is meant in a given line — 'karam' in the sense of divine grace (e.g. 'karam' bestowed by the Guru) comes from the Persian/Arabic side, not from the Sanskrit action/karma side, even though both spellings look identical in Gurmukhi.

context.note: A textbook case for why etymology must be checked per-occurrence rather than assumed from a single 'Punjabi meaning' — the same word carries two unrelated histories.

usageInContext.note: The surrounding grammar is the tell: when 'karam' is spoken of as something bestowed, given, or shown by the Guru/God (verbs like 'kita', 'dita', 'hoya'), it is almost always the Persian/Arabic 'grace' sense; when it is spoken of as something a person does or accumulates, it is the Sanskrit 'action' sense — the same spelling, resolved only by what verb is acting on it.
usageInContext.source: general grammatical pattern across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: grace or action, depending on the surrounding verb
usageInContext.bhavarth: a single Gurmukhi spelling silently carrying two unrelated histories, disambiguated only by its sentence, not by the word alone

interpretations.view: Consistent with his broader method of checking each Gurbani word against its own recurring usage, would treat 'karam' as requiring occurrence-by-occurrence disambiguation between its grace-sense and action-sense rather than one fixed translation.
interpretations.note: This is an inference from his general interpretive method, not a specific statement about this word — confirm before attributing it to him directly.

meaning: Illusion/worldly attachment — the enchanting but transient material world that veils the truth.

etymology.note: A core Vedantic term (the power that makes the illusory world appear real) absorbed wholesale into Bhakti poetry. Kabir ji's famous line describing Maya as a deceiver ('Maya maha thagni hum jani') uses the term exactly as Vedanta and the wider Bhakti tradition already understood it — Gurbani inherits, rather than redefines, this concept.

context.note: Best read against classical Vedantic philosophy, since that is the tradition that gives the term its force before Kabir or Guru Nanak ever used it.

usageInContext.note: Gurbani generally does not use 'Maya' to condemn the material world itself, but the attachment/forgetting it produces — the word's relational partner is almost always Haumai (the ego that clings) rather than the objects of the world themselves, which is why householders, not only renunciates, are addressed as capable of living beyond Maya.
usageInContext.source: recurring Maya/Haumai pairing across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: the clinging/forgetting it produces in the mind, not the material world as such

usageInContext.note: A famous Kabir couplet observes that Maya itself does not die, nor does the mind, even as generation after generation passes away trying to conquer it — the point being relational: it is the struggle between the two (Maya and mind) that Gurbani is diagnosing, not Maya as an isolated force.
usageInContext.source: Salok Kabir Ji, commonly cited across Sikh and Sant teaching
usageInContext.pankti: ਮਾਇਆ ਮੁਈ ਨ ਮਨੁ ਮੁਆ ਮਰਿ ਮਰਿ ਗਏ ਅਨੇਕ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: Maya has not died, nor has the mind died, though many have died trying, again and again
usageInContext.bhavarth: names an unresolved standoff between Maya and the mind, not a one-sided villain to be defeated

interpretations.view: Reads 'Maya' as attachment and self-deception rather than a condemnation of worldly life itself, consistent with Sikhi's general endorsement of the householder path (grihasti) over renunciation.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position, broadly shared across mainstream Sikh commentary — confirm his specific wording before quoting it as his.

meaning: Egotism, self-centeredness — the 'I-am-me' sense that Gurbani names as the root spiritual obstacle.

breakdown.meaning: "I" (from Prakrit अहं ahaṁ, ultimately Sanskrit अहम्)
"me" — an emphatic doubling of the first person

etymology.note: Rather than borrowing the Sanskrit philosophical term 'ahamkara' (अहंकार, ego-principle) directly, Gurbani builds its own compound out of everyday Punjabi/Prakrit first-person words, doubled for emphasis — a native coinage naming the same problem Sanskrit philosophy calls ahamkara.

context.note: One of the few core terms that is a home-grown Gurbani compound rather than a direct Sanskrit or Persian loan, though it parallels the older Sanskrit concept of ahamkara.

usageInContext.note: Named as what is dissolved by grasping Hukam (Japji Sahib Pauri 1), what Manmukh is defined by, and what the Panj Chor exploit — the same word functions as the hinge connecting several other entries in this dictionary rather than standing as an isolated fault.
usageInContext.source: recurring role across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: a hinge-concept, defined by what dissolves it (Hukam) and what it produces (Manmukh-ness, vulnerability to the Panj Chor)

usageInContext.note: A widely cited couplet frames Haumai as a chronic illness whose remedy is nonetheless already contained within it — the cure is not the removal of selfhood from outside, but living by the Guru's Shabad, again tying this entry back to Shabad.
usageInContext.source: a well-known couplet on Haumai, commonly cited across Sikh teaching (Guru Amar Das Ji)
usageInContext.pankti: ਹਉਮੈ ਦੀਰਘ ਰੋਗੁ ਹੈ ਦਾਰੂ ਭੀ ਇਸੁ ਮਾਹਿ ॥ ਕਿਰਪਾ ਕਰੇ ਜੇ ਆਪਣੀ ਤਾ ਗੁਰ ਕਾ ਸਬਦੁ ਕਮਾਹਿ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: Haumai is a chronic disease, but its remedy is also within it — if He shows His grace, one lives by the Guru's Word
usageInContext.bhavarth: the cure for ego is not its external removal but living by the Shabad, making the disease and its remedy inseparable

meaning: Natural spiritual equipoise — a state of effortless, innate balance and calm.

etymology.rootForm: सहज (sahaja) — "born together with, innate, natural" (सह saha "with" + ज ja "born")
etymology.note: Before Sikhi, 'Sahaja' was already a key term of the Nath yogis and the Sahajiya Bhakti-Tantric currents that also shaped Kabir ji (himself in dialogue with Nath tradition). Gurbani takes this pre-existing yogic-Bhakti term for spontaneous inner balance and repositions it as the fruit of Naam-simran rather than of yogic technique.

context.note: Understanding 'Sehaj' benefits from knowing the Nath/Sahajiya background Kabir was answering, not just the later Sikh sense of the word.

usageInContext.note: Where Nath-yogic usage ties Sahaja to a technique attained through withdrawal and yogic discipline, Gurbani's usage relocates it to ordinary lived life sustained by Naam-simran — the same word, but its route to attainment is relationally redefined against the Nath source it came from.
usageInContext.source: contrast between Nath-yogic usage and Gurbani usage
usageInContext.bhavarth: attainable through remembrance in ordinary/householder life, not only through yogic technique or renunciation

interpretations.view: Frames Sehaj as a steady inner poise reachable within ordinary householder life, in line with Sikhi's general position against renunciation as a requirement for realization.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position, broadly shared across mainstream Sikh commentary — confirm his specific wording before quoting it as his.

meaning: Unstruck — the 'unstruck celestial melody,' an inner mystical sound heard without any physical instrument striking it.

etymology.rootForm: अनाहत (anāhata) — "unstruck"; from the older yogic term अनाहत नाद (anāhata nāda, "unstruck sound")
etymology.note: A term from Nath-yogic and Upanishadic meditative tradition describing a mystical inner sound not produced by any physical collision (as ordinary sound is). Kabir ji, closely engaged with Nath yogis, uses 'Anhad' in this same inherited sense; Gurbani continues it as a metaphor for the constant, unproduced presence of the Divine.

context.note: Its full meaning is only visible against the yogic anāhata-nāda concept it comes from.

usageInContext.note: Usually paired with 'Shabad' (as 'Anhad Shabad') — the unstruck sound is specifically identified with the Guru's Word rather than left as a generic mystical experience, tying the term back to a word this dictionary already covers.
usageInContext.source: recurring "Anhad Shabad" phrase pattern
usageInContext.bhavarth: the constant, self-existing presence of the Word, described through the image of a sound with no physical cause

meaning: Nectar of immortality — used for the Guru's Word/Naam as spiritually life-giving, and later for the initiation nectar of the Khalsa.

etymology.note: Rooted in the old Vedic myth of the churning of the ocean (Samudra Manthan) that produces amrita, the drink of the gods' immortality. Bhakti and Sikh usage repurpose the word metaphorically — the Guru's Word or Naam as the true 'nectar' — rather than referring to the myth literally.

context.note: Its 'old-times' resonance goes back to Vedic mythology; the later Khalsa initiation sense (1699) is a distinct, additional historical layer on top of that older meaning.

usageInContext.note: The word carries two layers that must be told apart by date and context: in Gurbani text itself it is almost always the Guru's Word/Naam described metaphorically as nectar; in post-1699 Khalsa usage it additionally names the specific initiation liquid — the earlier metaphorical sense does not disappear, but a second, ritual-specific sense is layered on top of it.
usageInContext.source: contrast between Gurbani-era usage and post-1699 Khalsa usage
usageInContext.bhavarth: primarily a metaphor for the Word's life-giving effect; additionally, after 1699, a specific initiation rite

meaning: The 'Five Thieves' — Kaam (lust), Krodh (anger), Lobh (greed), Moh (attachment), and Hankar (pride), named as the five inner vices that rob a person of virtue.

etymology.note: The five vices themselves (Kaam, Krodh, Lobh, Moh, Hankar) are individually old Sanskrit ethical/psychological terms found broadly in Indian moral philosophy; Gurbani's contribution is naming the set together as 'thieves' who steal one's spiritual worth.

context.note: Each of the five component words can itself be looked up as a separate old Sanskrit ethical term; the group-metaphor of 'thieves' is the Gurbani framing layered on top.

usageInContext.note: The 'thieves' image only works in relation to a household they are robbing — that household is Haumai's domain; the metaphor's force comes from reading Panj Chor and Haumai together, not from the five vices as an abstract ethical list.
usageInContext.source: recurring imagery across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: what Haumai leaves vulnerable to being robbed, rather than five independent moral failings

meaning: The 'pure ones' — the collective body of initiated Sikhs, belonging directly to the Guru/God with no intermediary.

etymology.note: In Mughal administrative Persian, 'khalisa' land meant crown land held directly by the emperor, with no intermediary landlord. Guru Gobind Singh Ji repurposed this exact administrative image in 1699: the Khalsa belongs directly to the Guru/Akal Purakh, with no intermediary — a political-era word given a spiritual reframing.

context.note: A precise example of Mughal-Persian court vocabulary being repurposed for a Sikh institutional concept, in the same way 'hukam' was repurposed a century earlier by Guru Nanak.

usageInContext.note: Occurrences of the root sense 'khalis' (pure/unmixed) before 1699 do not yet carry the later institutional meaning of a formally initiated collective — reading an early use of the plain word as if it already meant "the Khalsa panth" would be an anachronism; the institutional sense is a specific historical addition on top of the older adjective.
usageInContext.source: contrast between pre-1699 and post-1699 usage
usageInContext.bhavarth: the institutional sense (a directly-Guru-owned collective) is a 1699 addition, not present in earlier occurrences of the plain word

interpretations.view: Emphasizes 'Khalsa' as naming a direct, unmediated relationship with the Guru/Akal Purakh — an inner sovereignty and discipline — rather than reducing it to external identity markers alone.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact wording against his lectures before quoting it as his.

meaning: Selfless service, performed without expectation of reward.

etymology.note: A general Sanskrit devotional term (service to a deity, teacher, or elder) common across Indian religious traditions well before Sikhi, which Gurbani elevates into a core spiritual discipline alongside Naam and Sangat.

context.note: Institutionalized in practice (langar, communal labor) but the word itself is common Sanskrit-Bhakti vocabulary, not a coinage.

usageInContext.note: Paired with Satguru ('Satgur ki seva') as much as with Sangat/Langar — the word covers both service directed at the Guru/teaching and service directed at the community, and which relationship is meant depends on what noun 'seva' is attached to in the line.
usageInContext.source: recurring phrase patterns across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: either devotion-in-action toward the Guru, or practical service to the community — decided by its paired noun, not the word alone

usageInContext.note: Ties Seva directly to a stated outcome (a seat in the Divine court) rather than leaving it as an abstract virtue — the couplet's logic is practical and consequential, not merely inspirational.
usageInContext.source: Japji Sahib, Pauri 21
usageInContext.pankti: ਵਿਚਿ ਦੁਨੀਆ ਸੇਵ ਕਮਾਈਐ ॥ ਤਾ ਦਰਗਹ ਬੈਸਣੁ ਪਾਈਐ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: Do seva in this world, and you shall find a seat in the Divine Court
usageInContext.bhavarth: seva as the means, not merely a virtue in itself — stated as a direct cause of a specific result

meaning: The free community kitchen where all sit and eat together as equals.

etymology.rootForm: لنگر (langar) — originally "anchor," extended in Persian/Ottoman-Sufi usage to mean a hospice or public kitchen attached to a Sufi shrine
etymology.note: Before Sikhi, 'langar' already denoted the free kitchens attached to Sufi hospices across the Persian-influenced Islamic world — the institution and its name both predate Guru Nanak. Sikhi adopts the existing Sufi-Persian institution and its name, then universalizes it by removing caste and hierarchy from who may sit and eat.

context.note: A strong example of a term whose 'old times' context is Sufi Persian hospitality practice, not Punjabi or Sanskrit.

usageInContext.note: The Sufi-hospice source institution served travelers and the poor generally; Sikhi's specific addition, when Guru Amar Das Ji institutionalized 'pehle pangat, phir sangat' (first sit together to eat, then the congregation), was making shared eating a precondition for the caste-mixed Sangat that followed — the word's Sikh meaning is bound to that sequencing, not just to charitable feeding.
usageInContext.source: Guru Amar Das Ji's institutionalization of Sangat–Langar practice
usageInContext.bhavarth: a precondition for caste-equal congregation, not only an act of charity

meaning: Devotional singing — chanting/singing the praises of God, typically to raag (musical measure).

etymology.note: A standard Sanskrit Bhakti term for singing praise (as in the wider 'kirtan/sankirtan' devotional-singing movements across India, e.g. among Vaishnava Bhakti groups) adopted directly, with Gurbani's own raag-based musical structure layered onto the practice.

context.note: Shares its root and general practice with the broader pan-Indian Bhakti devotional-singing tradition.

usageInContext.note: Distinguished from Paath by mode, not content — the same Shabad can be recited as Paath or sung as Kirtan; the raag heading placed over a shabad in Guru Granth Sahib signals that Kirtan, not silent reading, is its intended mode.
usageInContext.source: raag-heading structure of Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: a mode of engaging a Shabad (singing to raag) rather than a separate category of content from Paath

usageInContext.note: A well-known line values Kirtan by comparison — calling it a priceless jewel — placing its worth in relation to worldly treasure rather than describing it in purely musical or ritual terms.
usageInContext.source: a widely cited line on the value of Kirtan
usageInContext.bhavarth: valued by comparison to treasure, framing Kirtan's worth in economic/relational terms rather than describing the practice itself

meaning: Reading/recitation of scripture (Guru Granth Sahib).

etymology.note: A generic Sanskrit word for textual recitation, used across Indian religious traditions for reading their own scriptures; Sikhi applies the same generic term to reading Guru Granth Sahib.

context.note: Not a specialized coinage — its plain meaning ('reading/recitation') is unchanged from general Sanskrit-derived usage.

usageInContext.note: The word by itself is neutral about whether the reading is understood; whether a given Paath is 'arth sahit' (with meaning/understanding) or purely mechanical recitation is added by a qualifying word, not by 'Paath' alone.
usageInContext.source: general liturgical usage
usageInContext.bhavarth: neutral by itself — understanding vs. rote repetition is a distinction added by other words, not inherent to 'paath'

interpretations.source: Dharam Singh (Sach Khoj Academy) / Missionary College tradition
interpretations.view: Strongly emphasizes 'arth sahit paath' — reading with comprehension of meaning — over mechanical or purely ritual recitation, a position broadly associated with the Sikh Missionary College reform tradition.
interpretations.note: General, widely-documented position of this reform tradition — confirm his specific wording before quoting it as his personally.

meaning: Wonder, awe — the state of amazed astonishment at the vastness of creation, central to Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib.

etymology.note: A Sanskrit aesthetic/emotional term (one of the classical rasas, adbhuta-rasa, is built on the same root) that Guru Nanak develops at length in the 'Vismaad' passages of Japji Sahib describing awe at the scale of creation.

context.note: Best understood alongside the older Sanskrit aesthetic theory of wonder (adbhuta-rasa) that supplies its emotional register.

usageInContext.note: In Japji Sahib, the word is repeated in a cascading list ('Vismaad naad, vismaad ved...') rather than defined once — its meaning accumulates through repetition across many different objects of wonder (sound, scriptures, forms, colours, creatures), so no single line carries its full sense alone.
usageInContext.source: Japji Sahib, Pauri 16 (the Vismaad pauri)
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: Wonder at the sound-current, wonder at the scriptures
usageInContext.bhavarth: a sense built cumulatively across a whole list of wondered-at things, not fixed by any one occurrence

meaning: Void, emptiness — the primordial state before creation, described as 'Sunn Samadhi' (absorption in the void).

etymology.note: The same term used in classical Indian mathematics (zero) and in Buddhist/Vedantic philosophy (emptiness) and in Nath-yogic cosmology for the state before manifestation. Guru Nanak's 'Sunn Samadhi' draws directly on this shared Nath-yogic/Vedantic cosmological vocabulary, again reflecting Kabir's and the Naths' influence on the era's spiritual language.

context.note: Read together with 'Sehaj' and 'Anhad' — all three are part of the same inherited Nath-yogic cosmological vocabulary describing pre-creation and meditative states.

usageInContext.note: Appears in Gurbani both as a cosmological description (the pre-creation state) and as a meditative goal ('Sunn Samadhi'); the same word names both the beginning of time and a state a person can inwardly return to, and which sense applies depends on whether the surrounding lines are cosmological narrative or address to the practitioner.
usageInContext.source: recurring cosmological/meditative dual usage across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: either the pre-creation cosmological state, or an inwardly-accessible meditative absorption — decided by whether the passage is narrating origins or addressing the seeker

meaning: Ever-present, right beside one — as close and constant as one's own limb.

breakdown.meaning: limb, part of the body (Sanskrit aṅga)
with, together, in the company of (Sanskrit saṅga)

etymology.note: The phrase leans on the intimacy of 'ang' (a limb, inseparable from the body) to describe God's constant nearness — a vivid, physically-grounded image built from two ordinary Sanskrit-derived words.

context.note: A simple compound whose force comes from the everyday bodily meaning of 'ang' rather than from any specialized philosophical vocabulary.

meaning: Teacher — one who removes the darkness of ignorance; used for the ten Sikh Gurus, for God, and for the Guru Granth Sahib.

etymology.note: A pan-Indian term of long standing, used for teachers across virtually every Indian religious tradition (Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Sikh). Note: the popular folk breakdown 'gu' (darkness) + 'ru' (light/remover) is a widely repeated devotional gloss, not an attested Sanskrit grammatical derivation — worth knowing the difference between the folk etymology and the linguistic one.

context.note: Predates Sikhi by many centuries; Sikhi's distinctive contribution is investing the title in a line of ten human Gurus and then in the scripture itself (Guru Granth Sahib), not the word's origin.

usageInContext.note: The referent shifts across the ten Gurus, the Shabad/teaching itself, and finally the scripture (Guru Granth Sahib) — the same word tracks a historical transfer of authority from person to text, so which referent is meant depends on the period and genre of the passage using it.
usageInContext.source: transfer of Guruship across Sikh history (culminating 1708)
usageInContext.bhavarth: traces a historical transfer of authority (person → teaching → text), not one fixed referent

usageInContext.note: Guru Nanak's closing Salok of Japji Sahib uses 'Guru' metaphorically for air itself, alongside water as father and earth as mother — showing that even within Gurbani, 'Guru' is not reserved only for a human teacher but can name whatever sustains life.
usageInContext.source: Japji Sahib, closing Salok
usageInContext.pankti: ਪਵਣੁ ਗੁਰੂ ਪਾਣੀ ਪਿਤਾ ਮਾਤਾ ਧਰਤਿ ਮਹਤੁ ॥
usageInContext.shabdarthHere: Air is the Guru, Water the father, and the great Earth the mother
usageInContext.bhavarth: a metaphorical widening of 'Guru' to the elemental forces sustaining life, distinct from its usual sense of a personal teacher

interpretations.view: Distinguishes devotion to the Guru's wisdom/Shabad from veneration of a person's individual personality, cautioning against readings that centre the Gurus' historical persons over the teaching itself.
interpretations.note: General, publicly-known position — confirm exact wording against his lectures before quoting it as his.

meaning: Lord, God — a common, everyday Punjabi word for God, especially prominent in Baba Farid Ji's compositions.

etymology.note: A core Qur'anic/Islamic term for God, carried into Punjabi through Sufi devotional usage. Baba Farid Ji, a Sufi saint whose bani appears in Guru Granth Sahib, uses 'Rabb' exactly as it functions in Islamic devotional Punjabi and Arabic-Persian Sufi poetry — its meaning should be read through that Sufi-Islamic tradition, not translated as if it were a Sanskrit-rooted Hindu term.

context.note: The clearest single example in this dictionary of the principle that a word's source-language tradition (here, Arabic/Sufi) determines its correct reading, distinct from the Sanskrit-rooted terms used elsewhere in Guru Granth Sahib.

usageInContext.note: Sits in a plainer, more intimate register than 'Waheguru' or 'Nirankar' — Baba Farid Ji's shaloks use 'Rabb' the way ordinary Punjabi Sufi speech would, addressing God as one addresses a near, personal Sustainer, in contrast to the more formal Sanskritic register of Guru Nanak's Mool Mantar attributes describing what God is not.
usageInContext.source: contrast between Baba Farid Ji's shaloks and the Mool Mantar's register
usageInContext.bhavarth: an intimate, everyday address, in a different register from the Sanskritic philosophical vocabulary used elsewhere in the same scripture

meaning: The Timeless Being — God beyond the reach of death and time.

etymology.note: Purusha is an old Vedantic/Samkhya philosophical term for the primal conscious being/self. Prefixing 'Akal' (beyond time) turns a philosophical category already present in classical Indian thought into a direct name for God.

context.note: Especially prominent in Guru Gobind Singh Ji's Dasam Bani (as in the Chaupai Sahib's 'Akal Purakh ki rachha humnai'), where it functions almost as a personal, invocable name for God, distinct from its more descriptive Mool Mantar cousin 'Akal Murat.'

usageInContext.note: Related to, but distinct from, 'Akal Murat' in the Mool Mantar — 'Murat' (form/likeness) and 'Purakh' (being/person) frame the same timelessness two different ways: one denies God a shape, the other affirms God as a conscious being who can be addressed and invoked.
usageInContext.source: contrast between the Mool Mantar's 'Akal Murat' and later 'Akal Purakh' usage
usageInContext.bhavarth: a personal, invocable name for God, distinct from the more abstract Mool Mantar description

meaning: Sacred utterance/composition — the compositions of the Gurus and Bhagats collected in Guru Granth Sahib; 'Gurbani' specifically means the Guru's own utterance.

etymology.note: An old Sanskrit term for speech/voice (also a name for Saraswati, goddess of speech, in classical mythology). Gurbani narrows this general word for 'utterance' specifically to inspired, revealed composition.

context.note: Applied evenhandedly to Guru Bani and Bhagat Bani alike within Guru Granth Sahib — the term itself does not distinguish rank between a Guru's composition and a Bhagat's; both are simply 'bani.'

usageInContext.note: When prefixed 'Gur-' (Gurbani), the word narrows specifically to the Guru's own utterance; used alone, 'Bani' can refer inclusively to any inspired composition in the scripture, Bhagat or Guru — the prefix, not the root word, carries the distinction.
usageInContext.source: general usage pattern across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: inclusive of both Guru and Bhagat compositions unless narrowed by a prefix

meaning: A learner/disciple — one who follows and learns from the Guru's teaching.

etymology.rootForm: शिष्य (śiṣya, "disciple") or Pali/Prakrit सिख (sikkha, "instruction, training"; compare Sanskrit शिक्षा śikṣā, "education")
etymology.note: Scholars derive it from either root; both converge on the same sense of one who is being taught. The word predates any institutional identity — it simply names a learner in relation to a teacher, a relationship structure common across Indian religious traditions.

context.note: In Guru Nanak's own time, 'Sikh' described anyone learning from a Guru, without yet carrying the later institutional/communal identity that develops especially after 1699.

usageInContext.note: Its relational partner shifts across Sikh history: in early Gurbani a 'Sikh' is defined against the 'Guru' (a learner-teacher relation); after 1699 the same word increasingly overlaps with 'Khalsa' as a marker of formal, initiated identity — the word's scope widens from a relationship to a community.
usageInContext.source: historical shift across Sikh tradition
usageInContext.bhavarth: a relationship to a teacher, widening over time into a communal identity

meaning: Path/way — used for the Sikh community/tradition as a collective ('the Sikh Panth').

etymology.note: A common Sanskrit word for a literal path, used across many Indian religious traditions (a number of movements are called a 'panth') to mean a spiritual path or the community walking it — not a Sikh coinage, but adopted for the Sikh community collectively.

context.note: Gains its specific institutional sense ('the Khalsa Panth') especially from 1699 onward, layered on top of the older generic sense of any spiritual 'path/movement.'

meaning: Petition/supplication — the formal Sikh prayer of collective petition and remembrance.

etymology.rootForm: عرض داشت (ʿarẓ dāsht) — "a petition presented [to authority]"
etymology.note: An administrative Persian term for a formal petition submitted to a ruler or court, carried into Punjabi through Mughal-era bureaucratic usage — the same historical layer of Persian court vocabulary that gives Sikhi 'Hukam' and 'Khalsa.'

context.note: A clear parallel to Hukam and Khalsa: another Mughal-administrative Persian term repurposed for a specifically devotional Sikh practice — petitioning the Divine court rather than an earthly one.

usageInContext.note: The administrative root sense (a petition to a ruler) is preserved almost literally in devotional form: Ardas addresses Akal Purakh in the structure of a formal petition to a sovereign, which is part of why it closes by invoking the Guru's protection much as an earthly petition would invoke a patron's.
usageInContext.source: structural parallel between Persian court petitions and Sikh liturgical form
usageInContext.bhavarth: the same administrative structure of address, redirected from an earthly court to the Divine

meaning: A Guru's anniversary — a commemorative occasion marking a Guru's birth or another significant date.

etymology.note: 'Parva' is a standard Sanskrit word for a festival occasion or calendrical juncture, used across Indian tradition for religious festival-days generally; Sikhi attaches it to 'Guru' to mark the Gurus' own commemorative dates.

context.note: Not a scriptural term (it doesn't appear as Gurbani vocabulary) but a later calendrical/liturgical usage built from older Sanskrit festival vocabulary.

meaning: Throne/seat of authority — used for the five Takhts, the seats of temporal Sikh authority.

etymology.note: A standard Persian royal/administrative term for a monarch's throne, applied by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji (with the Akal Takht) to assert a seat of temporal Sikh authority standing alongside spiritual authority — drawing directly on Mughal-era Persian political vocabulary rather than a Sanskrit or Punjabi term.

context.note: Part of the same Persian-administrative vocabulary family as Hukam and Khalsa, here repurposed to assert political/temporal authority (miri) alongside spiritual authority (piri).

meaning: The Five Beloved Ones — the first five Sikhs initiated by Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1699, who offered their heads in devotion.

etymology.note: Two ordinary Sanskrit-derived words combined into a specific historical title; unlike Panj Chor (the Five Thieves, an inner vice), this 'Panj' names five actual historical people — the same numeral-compound pattern used for both abstract and historical reference.

context.note: A 1699 historical-institutional term, contemporary with Khalsa and distinct from earlier Gurbani vocabulary.

meaning: The practice of giving one-tenth of one's earnings/time for communal and charitable purposes.

etymology.note: Combines a Sanskrit numeral with an everyday Punjabi word for sharing/dividing — a practical, home-grown compound rather than a scriptural or Persian loan, reflecting institutional practice more than Gurbani vocabulary.

context.note: Develops as an institutional practice (linked historically to the masand/tithe-collection system) more than as a term found directly in Gurbani text itself.

meaning: Feet — used reverentially for the feet of the Guru/Divine, as in 'Guru charan,' a common image of humility and refuge.

etymology.note: An ordinary Sanskrit word for 'foot,' elevated by a widespread Indian devotional convention — touching or serving the feet of a revered teacher as the ultimate posture of humility — rather than by anything special to the word itself.

context.note: The reverence-for-feet convention is shared broadly across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and Sikh devotional cultures — Gurbani's 'charan' imagery continues, rather than originates, this custom.

usageInContext.note: Rarely stands for literal feet in devotional lines — it functions as a physical anchor for the more abstract idea of refuge/surrender, so 'seeking the Guru's charan' means seeking refuge and guidance, not a literal posture.
usageInContext.source: general devotional-imagery pattern across Guru Granth Sahib
usageInContext.bhavarth: a physical image standing in for refuge, humility, and surrender

meaning: Sight/vision — the act of seeing, and being in the presence of, the Guru or the Divine; also a general Indian philosophical term for a 'viewpoint' or system of thought.

etymology.rootForm: दर्शन (darśana) — "seeing, viewing; also, a philosophical system/viewpoint"
etymology.note: Carries a double sense already present in classical Sanskrit: literal seeing, and also each of the classical schools of Indian philosophy is itself called a 'darshan' (a way of seeing reality). Gurbani draws mainly on the devotional 'seeing the Divine/Guru' sense.

context.note: The devotional practice of seeking 'darshan' of a revered figure or shrine long predates Sikhi and is common across Indian religious life generally.

meaning: To chant, recite, or repeat — the discipline of repeated utterance, as in Japji Sahib ('the recitation of the Guru').

etymology.rootForm: जप् (jap) — "to utter in a low voice, recite repeatedly"
etymology.note: An old Sanskrit verbal root for repeated, often murmured recitation (as in 'japa' meditation across Hindu tradition), adopted directly as the title-action of Guru Nanak's opening composition, Japji Sahib ('Jap' plus the honorific suffix '-ji').

context.note: The same root/practice (repeated recitation) is common to Hindu japa-meditation traditions long before Sikhi; Guru Nanak's contribution is the content recited, not the practice-word itself.

meaning: Knowledge — spiritual/realized knowledge or wisdom, as distinct from mere information.

etymology.note: A core term of virtually every Indian philosophical school (jnana-marga, the 'path of knowledge,' is one of classical Hinduism's three major paths alongside bhakti and karma). Gurbani inherits the word and its weight, generally fusing it with devotion (bhagti) rather than treating it as a separate, purely intellectual path.

context.note: Best read against the older Hindu jnana-bhakti-karma framework it comes from — Gurbani tends to fuse rather than separate these, unlike some classical schools that rank them as distinct paths.

usageInContext.note: Frequently paired with 'Dhyan' (meditation/focus) as 'gian-dhyan,' suggesting the two are treated as a working pair — knowledge stabilized by sustained attention — rather than knowledge as a purely conceptual achievement on its own.
usageInContext.source: recurring "gian-dhyan" phrase pattern
usageInContext.bhavarth: realized understanding that depends on sustained attention (dhyan), not abstract information alone

meaning: Meditation, focused attention — sustained inner attention directed toward the Divine.

etymology.note: The same root that gives 'Zen' its name (via Chinese Chán, from Sanskrit dhyāna) — a term with a very wide footprint across Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain meditative traditions before Gurbani applies it to Naam-focused attention specifically.

context.note: A clear example of a word whose deep history runs through the entire subcontinent's meditative vocabulary, not through Punjabi or Sikh coinage.

meaning: Love — deep, devotional love for the Divine or Guru.

etymology.note: A standard Bhakti-movement term for devotional love, sharing its emotional register with the wider Krishna-bhakti and Sufi love-mysticism traditions that flourished alongside early Sikhi.

context.note: Kabir ji's use of 'prem' draws on the same Bhakti vocabulary of passionate divine love found in Vaishnava Bhakti poetry, later echoed in Gurbani's own emphasis on loving devotion over ritual.

usageInContext.note: Often intensified through the imagery of 'Birha' (the pain of separation from the Beloved) — Prem's full relational meaning in Gurbani and Sufi-influenced Punjabi poetry alike is completed by its shadow, the ache of longing, not by contentment alone.
usageInContext.source: shared Bhakti-Sufi imagery of love-in-separation
usageInContext.bhavarth: a love whose intensity is measured by longing (birha) as much as by union

meaning: The pain of separation/longing for the Divine Beloved — a central emotional theme in both Bhakti and Sufi Punjabi poetry.

etymology.note: A classical Sanskrit poetic term, central to Sanskrit and later Hindi/Punjabi love poetry generally (both human and divine), that becomes a major theme independently in both the Sant-Bhakti tradition (Kabir) and Punjabi Sufi poetry (Baba Farid, and later Bulleh Shah) — a rare case of one word carrying real weight in two distinct devotional streams within the same region.

context.note: Best read through both its Sanskrit-Bhakti and its Sufi-Punjabi life at once — the emotional charge of longing-for-the-Beloved is shared ground between the two traditions represented in Guru Granth Sahib.

meaning: Praise — used in the common Gurbani phrase 'Sifat Salah,' praise and glorification of God.

etymology.rootForm: صفة (ṣifa) — "attribute, quality, description"; extended in devotional Persian-Arabic usage to "praise"
etymology.note: An Arabic term for an attribute or descriptive quality, carried into Punjabi through Persian-Islamic devotional vocabulary — a direct parallel to Karam and Rabb as an Arabic-rooted term used matter-of-factly alongside Sanskrit vocabulary in the same scripture.

context.note: Regularly paired with 'Salah' (also Persian/Arabic in origin) as the fixed phrase 'Sifat Salah' — the pairing itself, not just the single word, is the meaningful unit.

usageInContext.note: Almost never occurs alone — it is bound to 'Salah' as a fixed phrase, so looking up 'Sifat' in isolation misses that its meaning is completed by its regular partner word.
usageInContext.source: fixed "Sifat Salah" phrase pattern
usageInContext.bhavarth: only fully meaningful as half of the bound phrase 'Sifat Salah'

meaning: Detachment — a state of dispassion toward worldly attachment, though in Gurbani often colored with longing rather than cold withdrawal.

etymology.note: A core term of classical Yoga and Vedanta philosophy (vairagya is one of the two pillars of yogic discipline alongside abhyasa/practice). Gurbani inherits the term but frequently merges it with devotional longing (closer to Birha) rather than keeping the more austere, renunciate sense it carries in classical Yoga.

context.note: Best read against its stricter classical-Yoga sense, to notice how Gurbani softens or redirects it toward loving longing rather than cold withdrawal from the world.

meaning: Truth, true being — the first substantive word of the Mool Mantar ('Sat Naam'), asserting that Truth is God's very name.

etymology.rootForm: सत् (sat) — "being, existing, true" (present participle of the root अस् as, "to be")
etymology.note: One of the most fundamental words in Sanskrit philosophy — grammatically, 'that which truly is' — used across Vedanta (as in sat-chit-ananda, being-consciousness-bliss) long before appearing as the opening substantive claim of the Mool Mantar.

context.note: Its philosophical weight (truth as a mode of being, not just factual correctness) comes directly from its long Vedantic history, not from Punjabi usage.

usageInContext.note: Immediately paired with 'Naam' as the Mool Mantar's second word, 'Sat Naam' — asserting not merely that God is true, but that Truth itself is how God is named and known, tying this word inseparably to Naam.
usageInContext.source: Mool Mantar
usageInContext.pankti: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ ਨਿਰਭਉ ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ ਅਜੂਨੀ ਸੈਭੰ ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ ॥
usageInContext.bhavarth: Truth as God's very Name/mode of being, not a separate descriptive attribute

meaning: 'Truth is the Timeless One' — now used as a common Sikh greeting, originally a martial declaration of faith.

etymology.note: Each component is individually old Sanskrit vocabulary already covered elsewhere in this dictionary (Sat, and the Akal of Akal Purakh); their combination into a set greeting phrase is a later Sikh development, not a single scriptural compound.

context.note: Historically linked to the battle-cry 'Jo Bole So Nihal, Sat Sri Akal' (associated with the Khalsa and the Sikh military tradition) before softening over time into an everyday greeting — a clear example of a phrase's register shifting from martial declaration to casual courtesy.

meaning: Victory — used in the Khalsa greeting 'Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh' (the Khalsa belongs to God, victory belongs to God).

etymology.note: A standard Arabic-Persian military/political term for conquest or victory, carried into Punjabi through the same Mughal-era administrative and martial vocabulary that gives Sikhi 'Hukam,' 'Khalsa,' and 'Takht.' Guru Gobind Singh Ji's formulation attributes the victory to God rather than to any worldly army, redirecting a term of earthly conquest toward the Divine.

context.note: Part of the same family of repurposed Mughal-Persian political/martial vocabulary as Khalsa, Hukam, and Takht — here, victory itself is reassigned from king or army to God.

meaning: The ceremonial sword, one of the Five Ks (Panj Kakar) worn by initiated Khalsa Sikhs, symbolizing dignity, self-defense, and the defense of the defenseless.

etymology.note: The 'Kirpa + Aan' breakdown (mercy joined to honor/dignity) is the widely circulated popular explanation of the name, presenting the sword as an instrument of compassionate protection rather than aggression — similar in status to the 'gu+ru' folk breakdown of 'Guru': a meaningful devotional gloss rather than a certain, formally attested linguistic derivation.

context.note: A 1699 Khalsa-institutional term, not found in Gurbani text itself, tied to the Panj Kakar (Five Ks) established at the founding of the Khalsa.
